headline: Creator of CI Kit & api-mock-services | Specializing in Developer Experience (DX), Local-First DevOps, and Green Container Tooling.

bios.oneLine: Open Source Architect building light, sustainable developer infrastructure and local-first CI/CD automation.
bios.short: Open Source Architect. Creator of CI Kit and api-mock-services — a local CI gate and a zero-dependency mock engine for payment, identity and messaging APIs. I publish how every number was measured, including the ones I threw away.
bios.long:
I am an Open Source Architect and developer tooling engineer working between Lagos and European time zones.

My work is in the unglamorous layer of developer infrastructure: the tools that decide whether a team waits forty seconds or forty minutes for a green build. I maintain two open-source projects.

CI Kit gives a repository a local gate that runs the same scripts its GitHub Actions workflow runs. It came out of an incident worth being honest about: 28 of the last 30 runs in a workspace had failed, and not one of them had failed on code — GitHub had been refusing to start the jobs over a spending limit, every run failing in about six seconds. Nobody could tell the difference between a red build and a build that never ran. The local gate answers the same question in about a hundred seconds, and it says why. I measured the honest version too: on identical work it takes 99 seconds on a laptop against 43–48 seconds on a GitHub runner. It is not faster. It is a guarantee of feedback, and the evidence document has a section on what is not claimed.

api-mock-services is one dependency-free Node process that stands in for eighteen third-party providers — Stripe, Paystack, Interswitch, Flutterwave, Monnify, YouVerify, Smile ID, Twilio, Resend, Xero and the rest. It replaced four containers: 50 MB against 250 MB, 0.0% idle CPU against 7.9%, and 1.4 seconds to the first request against 20 and rising. The footprint is a build gate, not a README claim — the build fails above 100 MB.

Both are MIT licensed, both publish their evidence, and both ship the harness that produced the numbers. I write long-form essays on CI/CD drift, offline-first integration testing and reproducible measurement, cross-posted to Substack and Dev.to, and I keep a public archive of everything I have written since 2013.

I am pursuing a Global Talent visa endorsement on the exceptional-promise stream, and this site — portfolio, writing, evidence and an endorsement evidence map in one place — is the artefact I would want assessed.

contentCalendar.topic: A red build is not always a red build
contentCalendar.hook: Our pipeline was red for a week. Not one of those 28 failures was a code failure — the jobs never started.
contentCalendar.body: GitHub had refused to start the jobs because of a spending limit. Every run failed in about six seconds. At the pull request level a red build is a red build, so the week looked like ordinary breakage. What I built to find out what was actually happening is now open source, and I wrote up the incident — including the measurement I threw away.
contentCalendar.cta: The full write-up, with the numbers and the harness, is on my site. Link in the comments.

contentCalendar.hook: Idle CPU, four mock containers vs one dependency-free process:
contentCalendar.body: 7.9% → 0.0%. Memory 250 MB → 50 MB. First request 20 s and rising → 1.4 s. Same mocks, one process, no dependencies. The footprint is a build gate now — the build fails above 100 MB, so the number cannot quietly stop being true.

contentCalendar.topic: Why the first mock arrangement was actively misleading
contentCalendar.hook: Our mock environment had 214 MB of memory dedicated to a proxy that never finished translating.
contentCalendar.body: Four containers, 250 MB, 7.9% idle CPU, and 20 seconds before the first request was answered. A test setup that permanently occupies a quarter of a gigabyte on a laptop is not a tool people use often — it is a tool people postpone. I wrote up how we got to one dependency-free process, and why 'no dependencies' is a policy rather than a preference.
contentCalendar.cta: Full architecture write-up on my site.

contentCalendar.body: Started this because I watched a team fail 28 builds in a row without anyone noticing the jobs had never run. Thank you to everyone who has filed an issue — particularly the ones that told me the toolchain check was hiding a class of real failures. Open to issues and PRs.
